summary: A 1969 note defining the format of host-to-host control messages. Each is a sequence of 8-bit bytes: a control byte followed by parameter bytes, and several messages may share a packet. It lists the nine control messages defined at that point, such as requests to set up connections.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers set up a conversation they swap small coded notes. This short 1969 memo lists the nine notes that existed at the time and says how each one is written so both sides read it the same way.

questions: how did early arpanet hosts set up connections
subtitle: How early ARPANET hosts sent control messages to set up and manage connections.

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET hosts needed a standard way to set up, manage, and tear down connections with each other.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 22 defines nine control messages (types 0-8), each consisting of a control byte followed by one or more parameter bytes. Messages can be sent together in a single packet.
tldr.outcome: This format was superseded by later, more comprehensive specifications, but established the pattern of control messages in host-host protocols.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 22 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was quickly followed by more comprehensive specifications, but its basic approach to control messaging persisted in ARPANET protocols.

sections.title: Control Message Format
sections.content: Host-to-host control messages consist of sequences of 8-bit bytes with a control byte followed by zero or more parameter bytes. Multiple control messages can be transmitted together in a single packet for efficiency. This format departs from the 7-bit ASCII character mode used in earlier specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A control message is like a short instruction: a code byte that says what kind of message it is, then some numbers that give details.

sections.title: Connection Establishment Messages
sections.content: At the time RFC 22 was written, nine control messages were defined. Type 0 requests a primary connection with a single link number parameter. Type 1 requests an auxiliary connection parallel to a primary link, with two parameters for the primary and auxiliary link numbers. Type 2 acknowledges a primary connection request from the other host, and type 3 acknowledges an auxiliary connection request. Type 4 rejects a primary connection request, and type 5 rejects an auxiliary request. These messages handle the initial setup and negotiation phase of host-to-host communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Some message types open a primary or parallel link. Others confirm or reject those requests.

sections.title: Link Control Messages
sections.content: Once a link is established, other control messages manage its operation. Type 6 is the CEASE directive, instructing the receiving host to stop transmitting on a specified link (flow control). Type 7 closes an output link and may be received before the last data packet arrives, since control messages take priority. Type 8 is UNCEASE, allowing transmission to resume on a previously ceased link. These messages provide dynamic control over data flow during the session.
sections.plainLanguage: After links are open, you can pause a link, close it, or restart it.
